idiom_name: plain object or class exposing the expected members (duck typing)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no interfaces at run time, so the target is whatever shape the caller uses: an adapter is a plain object or class that holds the adaptee and exposes the expected members, translating arguments and return values. Because property lookup is dynamic, nothing proves the adapter satisfies the shape - tests (or TypeScript via checkJs) do. A module-level wrapper function is often enough when only the call signature differs, and node:util.promisify is the library-provided special case of adapting an error-first callback API to promises. Avoid reaching for Proxy: intercepting property access is a different mechanism that changes access semantics rather than translating an interface.
pitfalls: Losing `this`: passing `adapter.method` as a callback drops the receiver - bind it or wrap it in an arrow function.
Spread/JSON.stringify copy only own enumerable properties, so an adapter built by spreading another object silently drops class behaviour; private fields (#x) are not visible to the spread at all.
Duck typing means a half-finished adapter still runs until the missing member is called: document the target shape and assert it in tests.
Wrapping an object that already satisfies the shape adds indirection and a second source of truth for the same interface.

variants.name: Callback-to-promise adapter (promisify style)
variants.implementation_notes: Error-first callbacks are adapted to promises by a closure that wraps the adaptee call in a Promise and maps (err, value) to reject/resolve; node:util.promisify does this generically for functions that follow the Node convention, and util.promisify.custom can register a bespoke adapter for APIs that do not. Use it to modernise a callback API without touching it, and hand-write the wrapper when the callback has multiple success values or a non-standard shape.
variants.idiom_name: new Promise((resolve, reject) => legacy.call(..., cb)) / util.promisify
pitfalls: A wrapper that ignores the callback's error argument leaves the promise pending forever.
util.promisify only understands the (err, value) convention; APIs with several success values or non-standard callbacks need a hand-written adapter.
Keep the adaptee call inside the Promise executor: a synchronous throw raised while building arguments outside it escapes as an exception instead of rejecting.
